explain: toString(2) writes a number in base 2: only 1s and 0s, the way the chip stores it.
builtFrom: a method call on a number, with the base as the argument
remember: The 2 is the base: 2 digits, 0 and 1.

explain: parseInt with 2 reads text of 1s and 0s back into a normal number.
example: Reading a binary number someone wrote down.
builtFrom: a function call with two arguments: the text and the base
remember: toString(2) goes number → bits, parseInt(…, 2) goes bits → number.

explain: padStart adds 0s to the front until the text is 4 long, so every number shows the same number of bits.
example: Hardware lessons: printing bits in tidy columns.
builtFrom: a string method with a length and the text to fill with
remember: Pad at the start, like the leading zeros on a car's mileage counter.

syntax: a & b   // AND: 1 only if both are 1
explain: One & works on bits: it gives 1 only when both bits are 1. It is an AND gate written as code. (&& is for true/false, & is for bits.)
example: Hardware lesson 2: logic gates. The carry in an adder.
remember: One & for bits, two && for true/false.

syntax: a | b   // OR: 1 if either is 1
explain: One | gives 1 when at least one bit is 1: an OR gate.
remember: The | is a wall with a gap on either side: either way gets through.

syntax: a ^ b   // XOR: 1 if they are different
explain: ^ is XOR (exclusive or): 1 when the two bits are different, 0 when they are the same. It is the sum bit when you add two bits.
remember: XOR asks "are they different?" 1 + 1 = 10 in binary, so the sum bit is 0.

explain: NOT turns 1 into 0 and 0 into 1. For a single bit, 1 - a does it simply.

syntax: (n >> i) & 1   // bit number i of n
explain: >> shifts the bits to the right by i places; & 1 then keeps only the last bit. Together they read one bit out of a number.
example: Hardware lesson 4: add two numbers with gates.
remember: Shift it to the end, then look at the end.
